references.text: In the preceding verse ([ref:Luk 20:14|Luke 20:14]), the vineyard workers decide to kill the heir, which leads directly to the action in verse 15 where they throw him out and kill him.

The parallel text in [ref:Matt 21:39|Matthew 21:39] describes the same event: "They seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him." Matthew emphasizes that the son was thrown out of the vineyard and then put to death.
The parallel text in [ref:Mark 12:8|Mark 12:8] states that they "seized him, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard." Mark has a slightly different order but refers to the same event.

[ref:Heb 13:12|Hebrews 13:12] says that "Jesus suffered outside the city gate in order to make the people holy through his own blood." The son being thrown out of the vineyard points prophetically to Jesus suffering outside Jerusalem, beyond the holy area.
[ref:Apg 7:58|Acts 7:58] tells us that Stephen was driven out of the city and stoned, a pattern that reflects the parable where the son is thrown out of the vineyard and killed.

In [ref:Matt 21:40-41|Matthew 21:40–41], Jesus asks the corresponding question about what the owner of the vineyard will do, and the listeners answer themselves that he will destroy those wicked men and lease the vineyard to others. This expands on the answer to Jesus' rhetorical question in Luke 20:15.

In [ref:Jes 5:3-5|Isaiah 5:3–5], the Lord asks a similar rhetorical question about what he should do with his vineyard that has not borne fruit. The parable of the vineyard in Luke builds on Isaiah's song of the vineyard and shares the thematic motif of judgment against unfaithful stewards.

The answer to the rhetorical question comes in [ref:Luk 20:16|Luke 20:16], where Jesus himself answers that the owner of the vineyard will come, kill those vineyard workers, and give the vineyard to others.

[ref:1 Tess 2:15|1 Thessalonians 2:15] refers to them "as those who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets and have persecuted us." Paul's words reflect the pattern of the parable where the vineyard workers kill both the servants and the son.
